absent: Locking, sleeping and concurrency rules for all fragments.
Signal delivery, masking, queuing and handler invocation semantics beyond numbers and layouts.
How and when each stat variant is selected and filled, and filesystem block accounting.
SVM VM control block layout and hypervisor exit handling flow beyond numeric codes and labels.
Byte-swap performance, availability to user versus kernel code, and 16-bit handling.
ucontext overall layout and extended state format.
x32 syscall table contents and vm86 enter/exit control flow and irq handling.

findings.text: x86 classic signals take small values in order: hangup takes value 1, interrupt takes value 2, quit takes value 3, illegal takes value 4, trap takes value 5, abort takes value 6, iot shares value 6, bus takes value 7, floating point takes value 8, kill takes value 9, user one takes value 10, segfault takes value 11, user two takes value 12, pipe takes value 13, alarm takes value 14, term takes value 15, stack fault takes value 16, child takes value 17, continue takes value 18, stop takes value 19, keyboard stop takes value 20, tty in takes value 21, tty out takes value 22, urgent takes value 23, cpu limit takes value 24, file size takes value 25, virtual alarm takes value 26, profiling takes value 27, window change takes value 28, io takes value 29 and poll aliases io.

Remaining signal ABI: power takes value 30, sys takes value 31, unused aliases sys at 31, first realtime takes value 32, last realtime equals the global signal count symbol, restorer flag takes value 0x04000000, minimum alternate stack takes value 2048 bytes and default alternate stack takes value 8192 bytes.

Two sigaction layouts are provided. One carries a two-way handler choice plus a mask plus flags plus a restorer callback, with friendly names mapping to the union members. The other carries a plain handler plus flags plus restorer plus mask, with commentary that the mask is deliberately last so the structure can grow.
Alternate signal stack is a three-member record aliased as stack_t: a user pointer for the base, an integer for flags, and a kernel size value for length.

Two word-size dependent stat layouts are provided. The 32-bit oriented one uses wide device, inode, device-id, size, block size and block count members, narrow mode and link and owner members, and second plus nanosecond pairs for access, modify and change times with two trailing spare wides. The 64-bit oriented one uses kernel long sized device, inode, link, device-id, size, block and time members, 32-bit mode and owner values, one explicit pad word and three trailing spares.

stat64 is a compatibility layout with 64-bit device and device-id, a 32-bit low inode plus a separate 64-bit full inode at the end, 32-bit mode and link, wide owner ids, signed 64-bit size, wide block size and 64-bit block count described as units of 512 bytes, second and nanosecond time pairs, and two four-byte pad areas.

Callers must clear padding before exposing stat records: one variant requires its two spare wides to be zero, another requires its pad word and three spares to be zero, and the 64-bit compatibility form requires both four-byte pads to be zeroed. Nanosecond timestamps are advertised as present.
The 64-bit compatibility stat form is marked as having a broken inode field, so consumers must use the trailing full inode rather than trusting the earlier narrow inode member alone.
Old kernel stat is a narrow legacy record using short integers for device, inode, mode, link, owner and device-id, with size and three timestamps that widen according to 32-bit versus 64-bit build.

SVM exit reasons are a dense numeric vocabulary. Control register reads and writes occupy the low range with selected registers only, debug register reads occupy the next block and writes the following block, exceptions span a 32-entry window starting at 0x40, interrupts and system events follow, descriptor table reads and writes are grouped, then single instruction and state intercepts continue through shutdown and virtualization instructions, with write traps for EFER and CR0 through CR15, plus sparse codes for invpcid, bus lock, idle halt, nested paging fault at 0x400, two AVIC codes and secure guest exit at 0x403.

Secure guest service numbers live near the top of 32 bits: mmio read and write, nmi completion, AP halt loop and jump table, page state change, guest requests, AP creation, VMPL run, SAVIC, hypervisor features query, termination request and unsupported event. Jump table get versus set and AP create versus destroy use tiny subcodes 0 through 2, SAVIC self uses all-ones, termination reason packs a 4-bit set and 8-bit code into low bits of exit info, software reserved base is 0xf0000000 and invalid guest state is all-ones.

A shared exit-reason table maps each numeric SVM and secure-guest code to a short diagnostic label, including per-exception labels formed by adding the CPU vector to the exception base and an invalid-state label for the all-ones code.

Two pure byte-reversal helpers are offered for 32 and 64 bit unsigned values. The 32-bit form reverses with one machine reversal. The 64-bit form uses one quad reversal on 64-bit builds and on 32-bit builds splits the value into two halves, reverses each half and exchanges them.
User context flags: extended state preservation takes value 1, signal-context stack flag takes value 2, strict stack restore takes value 4.
The x32 execution mode is distinguished by a high bit on the syscall number with value 0x40000000, and 32-bit compatible filesystem statistics use a packed four-byte aligned layout.
Each examined user header defines a single include-once guard macro so repeated inclusion is harmless.

VM86 ABI: BIOS segment takes value 0x0f000, CPU levels run from 0 for 8086 through 5 for 586, return codes are 0 for signal, 1 for unknown fault, 2 for software interrupt, 3 for virtual interrupt enable, 4 for pending PIC work and 6 for debugger trap, and control operations run 0 install check, 1 enter, 2 enter without bypass, 3 request irq, 4 free irq, 5 get irq bits, 6 get and reset irq.
A VM86 return word encodes outcome in its low byte and an argument such as interrupt number in its upper bits, with helpers to separate the two halves.

VM86 register state holds general registers, null placeholder selectors, saved system call number, instruction pointer, code selector with pad, flags, stack pointer and selector, plus v86-only data selectors each with padding. A revector bitmap holds eight words covering 256 interrupts. The base control block combines registers with flags, screen bitmap, cpu type and two revector maps; the plus variant adds force-return, debugger active and pending-trace bits plus a 32-entry debugger table.
